newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Crude Outlook - Discounts to reign supreme.
newsitem.headline: Asia Crude Outlook - Discounts to reign supreme.

text.p: Refinery margins were positive Monday, but traders said that would offer only a short-lived support for crude prices and the outlook for this week remained bearish.

"Given the real weakness of margins in the market, I don't think you will see much upturn. It could make a difference to players, like the Chinese, who are looking for fixed outright priced deals," one trader said.
Global futures prices fell sharply on Friday, extending the weakness seen earlier in the week.
Front-month NYMEX prices dropped to their lowest level in 15 months, while front-month Brent held its current trading range but could catch up soon.
July NYMEX crude fell 87 cents to $18.79 per barrel on Friday -- the lowest level since February 1996 -- and rebounded 12 cents to $18.91 on ACCESS on Monday.
July Brent was holding steady on SIMEX -- quoted but untraded at $17.70/$17.93 -- after dropping 62 cents in London on Friday to $17.70.
The fall in crude prices has prompted basic refinery margins to turn positive, offering some brief respite for beleagured refiners.
But traders said they expected product prices to fall in line with Friday's crude numbers and swing margins into negative territory again.

Traders said the weakness of refinery margins would keep prices under pressure. In addition, the Brent/Dubai spread remained narrow, which would keep the import window open for West African crude coming into Asia.
But technically, the lower outright values could generate some demand and help alleviate the contango in most crude markets.
Market sources said the deep discounts for spot trade, working on most Middle East grades, would continue this week.
Demand for heavier sweet regional grades failed to match expectations last week, allowing prices to turn lower.
This week, traders said they expected prices to hold steady amid a lack of incentive to move either way too dramatically.

Traders said demand was normal on a seasonal basis -- with the exception of a fall in demand from China. Supply was more limited now because the trading month was coming to an end, which would underpin current levels.
"I don't think there is much downside other than the discounts that you are looking at already," one trader said. "Most people are in the process of trading their barrels."
"But equally, if demand in North Asia does not improve, I don't think we will see an improvement as far as OSP-related deals are concerned," he said.
Minas was heard traded late last week as low as ICP -19/-20 cents per barrel. One trader said the price was exceptional, and instead he assessed the price at ICP -10/+10 cents.
One trader said China might well still look to buy more aggressively at the end of current-month trading or for July regional trading.
"It looks healthy. It is not fantastic, but China stocks are not so high to exclude them from taking barrels. It's the refinery economics that is worrying the Chinese," he said.
-- Singapore Newsroom (+65 870 3081)
